quote: than a mole sees through its own skin
note: Medieval natural history held that the mole's eyes were covered by a layer of skin, leaving it blind or nearly so.
Evening of Easter Monday, Dante's second day on the mountain. He has been inside the smoke of the angry since the end of Canto 15.

The faculty that forms pictures in the mind. Each terrace teaches by examples of its sin and of the opposite virtue. On this one they come as visions inside Dante's head: three scenes of gentleness in Canto 15, and now three of anger and the ruin it brings.

Normally the imagination works on what the senses give it. When it sees things the senses never supplied, Dante says, the images come from above: from the influence of the stars, or sent by God's will.

Procne, in Ovid's Metamorphoses. Her husband Tereus, king of Thrace, raped her sister Philomela and cut out her tongue. In revenge Procne killed their own small son and served him to his father as a meal. The gods turned them all into birds.

quote: the bird that most loves to sing
note: The nightingale. Ancient writers disagree about which sister became the nightingale and which the swallow. Dante seems to make Procne the nightingale.

Haman, chief minister of the Persian king in the Book of Esther. Furious that the Jew Mordecai would not bow to him, he plotted to have all the Jews of the empire killed. He was put to death on the gallows he had built for Mordecai. Dante's Latin Bible calls it a cross.
The king of Persia in the Book of Esther, often identified with Xerxes.

quote: Esther his wife, and righteous Mordecai
note: Esther was the king's Jewish queen and Mordecai her cousin and guardian. She revealed Haman's plot to the king and saved her people. The Jewish feast of Purim remembers it.

context: She weeps for her mother, who has just hanged herself. The scene is from the last book of the Aeneid.

note: Amata, wife of King Latinus. She wanted her daughter to marry the Italian prince Turnus, not the Trojan newcomer Aeneas. Wrongly believing that Turnus had been killed in battle, she hanged herself in a rage.
The irony of anger: Amata killed herself so as not to lose her daughter to Aeneas, and by dying lost her for good. All three visions show anger destroying the angry person or what that person loves.
The light of the angel who guards the way up from the third terrace. Every terrace ends with an angel, each too bright for Dante to look at.

quote: whoever sees need and waits to be asked
note: A proverb of courtesy that Dante also uses in his Convivio: real generosity gives before it is asked. The angel helps unprompted, the opposite of the angry spirit that holds back.
The law of the mountain, explained in Canto 7: no one can climb a single step after sunset. The sun stands for God's grace, and without it the will can do nothing.
At the gate of Purgatory an angel cut seven letter P's on Dante's forehead, one for each deadly sin (peccatum in Latin). The angel of each terrace brushes one away with his wing. This is the third.
One of the Beatitudes, the blessings that open Christ's Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:9). A different one is spoken at the exit of each terrace.
Dante's addition to the Gospel verse. Medieval teaching kept a place for good anger, the just indignation at wrong that Dante himself shows often in the poem. Only the bad kind is purged here.
Night has fallen and the law of the mountain takes hold: Dante's legs will not carry him further. It suits the place. They have reached the terrace of sloth.
The fourth of the seven terraces, the middle one. Its souls will not appear until the next canto.
Sloth, in Latin acedia. It meant more than laziness: a sluggishness of spirit, knowing the good and not caring enough to pursue it.
A rower who pulled too slowly must now make up the lost strokes.

quote: some useful fruit from our delay
note: While they wait for daylight, Virgil explains how Purgatory is organized. In Inferno 11 another forced pause was used the same way, to lay out the plan of Hell.
The heart of the poem's thought, placed at its center: this is Canto 51 of 100. All action comes from love, and every sin is love gone wrong. The seven terraces are sorted by the ways it goes wrong.

Natural love is the built-in pull of every creature toward its own good, like a stone falling or a plant turning to the sun. It can't be mistaken. Rational love, the love of the mind, involves choice, so it can be.
God. The secondary goods are the good things of this world, which are rightly loved in moderation.

quote: all things are safe from self-hatred
note: Virgil narrows the field. No creature can truly will its own harm, and none can hate God, the source of its being. So the only evil a person can love is harm to someone else.
Pride, purged on the first terrace (Cantos 10–12): wanting to stand highest by having others brought low.
Envy, purged on the second terrace (Cantos 13–14): resenting another's success as a loss to oneself.
Anger, purged on the third terrace, which the poets have just left: the hunger to pay back a wrong.
On the three terraces already climbed. Purgatory is ordered from the worst sins at the bottom to the lightest at the top, the reverse of Hell, where the worst lie deepest.
Sloth again, the sin of this middle terrace. It is the only one that is neither love of harm nor too much love of lesser things, but too little love of the true good, God.

quote: another good that brings no happiness
note: Worldly goods such as money, food and sex. They are real goods, but they can't satisfy the soul, and loving them too much is sin.
The terraces of avarice (Cantos 19–21), gluttony (Cantos 22–24) and lust (Cantos 25–27).
Virgil leaves Dante, and the reader, to work out the last three terraces by climbing them.
